title: Given a sorted array (or a sorted linked list), remove the duplicate elements in place so that each element appears only once, and return the new length (or the de-duplicated list). Solve it without allocating a second structure. (LeetCode: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List / Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array)
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Structure (Two Pointers, In Place)
keyPoints: In sorted data, duplicates are neighbours, so a single slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.
Slow pointer marks the end of the unique prefix; fast pointer scans ahead. When fast differs from slow, copy and advance slow.
The unique count is slow + 1; elements beyond slow are leftover garbage.
For a sorted linked list, walk a single pointer and unlink nodes whose value equals the current node's value.
The common variant allowing at most two occurrences compares fast against slow - 1 instead of slow.
O(n) time and O(1) extra space for both array and linked list versions.

s1_definition.oneliner: In sorted data, duplicates are neighbours, so one slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Remove Duplicates** – given a sorted array or linked list, remove duplicate elements in place so each value appears only once.
- **Slow-fast pointers** – slow marks the end of the unique prefix, fast scans ahead; when fast finds a new value, copy it to slow + 1.
- **Array version** – returns the new logical length; elements beyond slow are ignored.
- **Linked list version** – unlinks duplicate nodes by adjusting next pointers.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a sorted ledger of account numbers where the same account appears several times in a row because of repeated entries. He keeps one finger on the last unique account and reads forward with another finger. Whenever the reading finger sees an account different from the last unique one, he writes it right after his confirmed section and moves his confirming finger forward.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted structure in place relies on one key fact: because the data is sorted, every group of equal values sits together, so I only need to compare each element to the previous kept element. That lets me solve it in a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space using a slow-fast two-pointer scheme.

For the array version I keep a slow pointer at the last unique element and scan forward with a fast pointer. Whenever the fast element differs from the slow element, I advance slow and copy the fast element in, building the unique prefix in place. The unique count is slow + 1, and everything beyond that is leftover garbage. For the sorted linked list I walk a single pointer and unlink nodes whose value equals the current node's value.

The senior-level point is knowing the variants. If the requirement allows each element at most twice, I compare fast against slow - 1 instead of slow. For the harder linked-list variant that removes every node that ever had a duplicate, I use a dummy head so I have a stable handle before a run of duplicates.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this to clean a sorted feed of account numbers from a partner, where overlapping export windows produced repeats. The feed was large, so allocating a second array was not acceptable, and the in-place slow-fast sweep collapsed the repeats cheaply before reconciliation ran.

Remember one sentence: in sorted data, keep a slow pointer at the last unique element and advance it only when the fast pointer finds a new value, giving O(n) in-place deduplication.
